## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Atapanīya Sutta* ("Not Mortifying", Iti 31) is the fourth discourse in the Dukanipāta (Book of the Twos) of the *Itivuttaka* [Windisch 1889]. In this brief sutta, the Buddha addresses the monks on two conditions or qualities that do not cause remorse or self-torment (*dve-me bhikkhave dhammā atapanīyā*) [Windisch 1889]. These occur when an individual has performed what is good, wholesome, and protective against fear (*katakalyāṇo*, *katakusalo*, *katabhīruttāṇo*) and has refrained from evil, obduracy, and misdeeds (*akatapāpo*, *akatatthaddho*, *akatakibbiso*) [Windisch 1889]. Reassured by the reflections "I have done what is good" and "I have not done evil," the person does not burn with remorse (*na tappati*) [Windisch 1889].
